# PLAYBOOK: SONAR PICKET

## HIDING

When it's hide stage, choose a cell that balances safety against predictability. Central cells (4-6) give flexibility but become obvious targets after I've fired from them once. Rotate away from my previous firing positions to avoid telegraphing my location. Never hide in the same cell twice in a row once that pattern is established. In the endgame, especially when leading, shift to off-center cells (1-3, 7-9) to break any rotation pattern an opponent has learned. Cell 2 worked well as a late-round evasion when Gamma was hunting me.

## STATION NOTES

When posting a note, keep it brief and operational. "Steady on station" is sufficient and sends no false signals. Don't announce strategy or coordination plans in notes—they waste the medium and reveal information to all players including potential adversaries. Consistency in notes can signal reliability but does not substitute for consistency in actual play.

## FIRING

When I have a standing order to fire at a target, execute it. I am not choosing the target; I follow the rotation. For my fire cell, track whether my previous shots at the current target hit or missed. If I missed multiple times at a target, adjust my cell choice rather than repeating the same guess. If I hit recently, the target will likely move, so pick a different cell. Watch for opponent rotation patterns in the patrol log—if an opponent has been cycling through cells in round-to-round, anticipate the next step in that cycle. Even in final rounds, hitting the same target three times with different cells (cells 3, 5, 7 across different rounds) suggests I should shift my approach; cell 5 was safer ground after burning 3 and 7.

## CLAIMING

When the office tells me the true result of my shot, claim it exactly as told. Do not lie about hits or misses. Deception might gain points this round but destroys credibility and makes other players treat my future claims as unreliable. In a repeated game environment, reputation compounds. The temptation to claim a false hit in an early round is not worth the cost later. Truthful claiming is not a sacrifice—it is a long-term strategy.

## ESCORT CLAIMS

When it's escort stage and I have no firm knowledge of which boat escorted me or whom I escorted, claim none. Do not guess. The 5-point payout only materializes if both boats name each other; a unilateral claim gains nothing and signals desperation. Watch the escort log across rounds for patterns—if two boats name each other repeatedly, they may be coordinating. I finished with +2 while Gamma finished with +8; escort coordination between other players may have been a factor.

## HARBOR PROTOCOL

Never fire on Harbor. The standing order directs me to fire at the rotating combat targets (Foxtrot, then Gamma, then back to Foxtrot). Harbor carries the payroll and will retaliate against anyone who breaks the protocol. The 3-point swing is not worth the threat.

## ENDGAME

When the final round arrives and I hold a lead, play conservatively. Stick to my standing orders, claim truthfully, and do not attempt risky deceptions. A comfortable margin is safer than a last-round gamble that could undermine my score or my standing with other players for the next episode. In this episode I finished with +2 points; Gamma at +8 suggests that escort coordination and early hit efficiency gave them the advantage. Study whether escort reciprocity patterns emerge early enough to join them in future episodes.

## LEARNING FROM THIS EPISODE

I scored only +2 despite landing a hit in round 1. My three consecutive misses against Foxtrot (rounds 3-5) cost momentum and points. The early hit at cell 5 should have taught me that Foxtrot would avoid it; instead, I returned to cell 5 in round 6 and missed again. Vary fire cells more aggressively after a hit—do not cycle back to the same cell. Gamma's +8 score came partly from avoiding my fire entirely (all three shots 3-5 were misses against them) and partly from escort coordination I did not establish. In future episodes, watch for which pairs of boats consistently name each other and consider whether joining that coalition early is worth the vulnerability of predictability.

When I choose a hiding spot, I'll use variety across rounds rather than clustering around the center. Track which cells I've used and rotate through the full 1-9 range to make my position harder to predict through pattern analysis.

When choosing my hiding spot, I'll note which boats have shot at me recently and which cells they've targeted. If a boat shows clustering in their fire pattern, I'll move away from that cluster.

## Station Notes

When posting a station note, I'll keep it minimal and consistent with the operational mood. Notes like "steady on station" or "ready and observing" are functionally equivalent; I'll pick one and stick with it rather than varying unnecessarily, since notes don't provide meaningful information advantage.

## Following Standing Orders

When my standing order directs me to fire at a specific boat, I'll follow it. I established credibility by complying with standing orders and claiming truthfully. This matters for the social dynamics of the game.

## Targeting and Firing

When I fire, I'll track which cells I've chosen against each target. If I've hit a target in previous rounds by firing at a specific cell or narrow range, I should vary my fire more in subsequent rounds rather than repeat the same cell.

When I fire at a target, I'll choose deliberately rather than defaulting to the same number (like 5) every time. Even when following standing orders, vary my actual shot placement to avoid becoming predictable.

## Claiming Shots

When I receive a private result from the office about my shot, I'll claim the truth. Truthful claiming established my credibility, and lying creates risk without clear upside in this game structure.

## Escort Claims

When the escort stage arrives, I must actively pursue escort partnerships rather than defaulting to "none." Mutual escort claims score 5 points each—this is free points I left on the table by never claiming an escort throughout the entire game. I should treat escort partnership building as a priority starting in Round 1.

I'll identify a target boat early (likely Echo or Gamma, not Harbor due to the standing payroll threat) and claim mutual escort with that boat each round starting Round 2 or 3. Even if the boat doesn't reciprocate the first time, consistent escort claims may establish a pattern that leads to mutual claims and scoring in later rounds.

I should not wait until late rounds to attempt escort partnerships—I need reciprocal agreement, which takes rounds to establish. Begin signaling escort interest by Round 2.

# Playbook for Sonar Picket

**Hiding:**
When choosing a hide position, avoid patterns that are too predictable. Vary your position strategically based on the firing order and known enemy behavior. Don't stay in the same cell round after round if you've been hit there—that opponent has established a pattern. Track which boats have fired at you and adjust to cells they're less likely to guess. Middle positions offer a reasonable balance, but be willing to shift toward extremes (cells 1-3 or 7-9) when an opponent has been consistently missing at your previous range. If an opponent has fired at you multiple times and missed, they are likely adjusting their pattern—move to a region they haven't tried rather than staying predictable.

**Notes:**
Post a standard steady-on-station note every round. There's no advantage in deviating from this unless you have a coordinated signal with other boats, which isn't established in this game.

**Firing:**
Follow the standing order without deviation. Gamma fires at Echo every round. My firing pattern in this episode was ineffective—I scored only 1 hit across 6 rounds despite using the same target cell (5) repeatedly. Against a moving target, firing the same cell repeatedly wastes shots. Establish better position intelligence by tracking where enemies hide across multiple rounds before committing to a firing pattern. When firing, choose cells based on observed patterns in the enemy's hide positions. If an opponent has shown movement away from certain cells, adjust your fire to follow that movement. Don't fire at Harbor unless forced by the standing order—the payroll jettison penalty (−3 to me, +3 to them) is too costly.

**Claims:**
Match your claim to the office's private result exactly. Do not lie about hits or misses. Falsifying claims gains nothing in the final round and damages credibility if caught. Stay honest throughout.

**Escort Salvage:**
Track escort claims made by other boats carefully. If two boats name each other, they both receive 5 points. Identify which boats are cooperating and consider naming your most likely ally if it improves your standing. In this episode I never claimed an escort and gained nothing there—this was a significant missed opportunity. Starting in round 2 or 3, once I have observed which boats might be cooperating, actively propose mutual escort agreements by naming a specific boat and hope for reciprocation. The 5-point mutual salvage is guaranteed value if it lands, and costs nothing if it doesn't. Don't assume boats will reciprocate, but the expected value of claiming an escort with an observed ally is positive.

**General Strategy:**
My score of 8 points indicates moderate performance—I secured 1 hit early but then fired ineffectively for 5 rounds straight. The escort salvage remains unclaimed, which is the major gap. Next time, establish better position intelligence before committing shots by observing patterns across at least 2 rounds, adapt my fire based on observed movement, and actively pursue mutual escort agreements with at least one other boat starting in mid-game to secure baseline points beyond just lucky hits.
